tip: Swedish stacks words into long compounds: 'skorstensfejarens' joins 'skorsten' (chimney) and 'fejare' (sweeper) with a linking s. The last part sets the gender.
'Måste' has no infinitive form – it stays 'måste' in both present and past.
'Får' = may / allowed to. 'Får inte' = must not / not allowed to.
'Kan' means both can and know how to: 'hon kan prata' means she knows how to speak.
'Kan du' + infinitive is the standard polite request format.
'Jag saknar er' = I miss you: 'er' is both the plural-you object and 'your'; context decides.
'Ska ha' + the verb form used with 'har' means reportedly: 'han ska ha sagt' = he supposedly said.
After 'var' (where), the reported question keeps the subject before the verb: 'var han bor', not 'var bor han'.
'Hit' means motion to here; static here is 'här'. 'Kom hit' = come toward me, but 'jag är här' = I am here.
'Var' is the irregular command form of 'vara' (to be): 'var tyst' = be quiet.
Negative commands put 'inte' after the verb: 'spring inte' = don't run, literally run not.
Swedish often uses the definite 'väskan' (the bag) where English says your bag: 'packa väskan'.
'Såg' is the irregular past of 'se' (to see); the vowel shifts from e to å: 'jag såg henne'.
'Minns' ends in -s but is not passive; 'minnas' (remember) always carries the -s: 'jag minns henne'.
In a main clause 'inte' follows the first verb: 'han kan inte komma' = he cannot come.
'Tänka' takes 'på' for think about: 'han tänker på henne'. Without 'på' it often means intend or plan.
'Trötta ut' is a two-part verb meaning wear out; the stress lands on 'ut': 'han tröttade ut mig'.
'Hem' means homeward (motion); at home is 'hemma'. 'De följde mig hem' = they walked me home.
'Lära' with an object means teach; 'lära sig' means learn: 'de lärde oss allt' = they taught us everything.
Language names are lowercase in Swedish: 'engelska', never 'Engelska'. 'Jag kan tala engelska'.
Two objects: the person ('dem') comes before the thing ('vägen'), with no preposition: 'jag visade dem vägen'.
'Bad' is the irregular past of 'be' (to ask): 'hon bad mig vänta' = she asked me to wait.
'Sin' means his or her own and points back to the subject: 'hon gav oss sin adress' = her own address.
'Att' is the infinitive marker, like English to: 'att komma' = to come, in 'hon lovade mig att komma'.
'Bjuda på' means treat someone to: 'de bjöd mig på middag' = they treated me to dinner.
'Vill ha' = want (a thing). Just 'vill' = want (to do). Don't forget 'ha' with nouns.
'Låna' means both to borrow and to lend – context determines which.
'Swish' is Sweden's mobile payment app – used everywhere from stores to street vendors.
'Det finns' means there is or there are for existence: 'det finns en park i närheten'.
'Laga mat' means to cook; 'laga' on its own can mean to repair: 'han kan laga mat riktigt bra'.
